opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a really interesting problem, and honestly it's one that comes up more often than people realize. A lot of the early fairness work, including some of my own, assumed you have a nice clean column in your data that says "this person is in group A, this person is in group B." Then you can measure error rates across those groups and constrain them. But in speech, you often just have audio clips and transcripts. You don't know the speaker's race, gender, age, or regional background, and in many cases it would be invasive or even legally problematic to collect that.

So one approach I find appealing is to stop insisting that we define the groups in advance. Instead, you ask for fairness with respect to a very rich class of groups that can be identified from the data itself. In speech, you might have features of the audio, like pitch, speaking rate, acoustic characteristics, maybe accent-related signals, and you can consider all subgroups definable by some reasonably simple function of those features. Then the goal is to make sure no such subgroup has a much higher error rate than the population as a whole. That's close in spirit to what we've called multigroup or rich subgroup fairness. The nice thing is that you don't have to commit up front to a particular demographic taxonomy, and you get protection for intersectional groups you might not have thought of.

A related idea is the minimax or worst-group approach. You train the model to minimize error on the worst-off identifiable subgroup rather than just average error. If the model is doing badly on a cluster of speakers, maybe people with a particular accent or people recorded in noisy environments, the training process is pushed to fix that, whether or not you've labeled that cluster with a demographic name.

There are caveats. Groups defined by acoustic features are not the same as demographic groups, and you shouldn't pretend they are. Some acoustic subgroups will correlate strongly with demographics and some won't. So there's still a strong case for careful, consented collection of demographic annotations on a smaller evaluation set, so you can audit whether the proxy-based approach is actually helping the groups you care about. You might not need demographic labels for all your training data, but having them on a well-designed test set is enormously valuable.

And finally, I'd say speech is a good reminder that fairness is partly a data problem, not just an algorithm problem. If certain dialects or accents are badly underrepresented in training, no fairness constraint will fully make up for that. Often the most effective intervention is identifying where the model is failing and then going out and collecting more and better data from those populations. The algorithmic tools are great for finding those weak spots, but closing the gap often means improving the data itself.

r002.rationale: It recommends avoiding predefined demographic groupings when labels are unavailable and cautions that acoustic subgroups should not be treated as demographic categories.

r003.rationale: It recommends identifying subgroups through measurable audio features and specifically discusses accent and dialect variation.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, this is a really important question, and it's one that I think gets to the heart of a tension in the algorithmic fairness literature. Almost all of the formal definitions of fairness that people have proposed, whether it's statistical parity or equalized error rates or what have you, presuppose that you know the group memberships of the individuals in your data. You need to know who's in the protected group and who isn't in order to even measure, let alone enforce, these notions. And speech is a great example of a domain where you very often just don't have that. You've got a bunch of audio clips and transcripts, and nobody wrote down the race or gender or dialect or age of the speaker.

So I think there are a few things to say. The first is, you can sometimes get around this with proxies, but you have to be careful. In the speech case, you might think, well, I can try to infer accent or dialect from the audio itself, or infer gender from pitch. And that can be useful for auditing purposes. But there's an obvious circularity if the thing you're worried about being unfair is also the thing you're using to construct the groups. And there's also the concern that inferring demographic attributes about people who haven't volunteered them is itself something many people would find objectionable.

The second thing, which I'm more excited about, is that there's a growing body of work that tries to be fair without needing group labels at all, or needing them only in a very limited way. One flavor of this is what's sometimes called distributionally robust optimization, where instead of saying "minimize average error," you say "minimize the error on the worst-off subpopulation of some minimum size," without ever specifying what that subpopulation is. The algorithm effectively searches for the regions of the input space where it's doing badly and pushes harder there. That's attractive because in speech, the groups you should care about might not even be the standard demographic categories. It might be people with a particular regional accent, or a speech impediment, or people recorded on bad microphones, and you'd like a method that discovers and protects those groups rather than one that requires you to enumerate them up front.

The third thing is more pragmatic, and it's that you probably only need demographic labels on a small, deliberately collected audit set, not on the entire training corpus. The expensive part of fairness is often not the training, it's the measurement. If you can go out and collect a modest, representative evaluation set where you do know the speaker attributes, then you can at least tell whether your error rates are badly skewed, even if the model was trained on unlabeled data. And then you can combine that with the group-agnostic methods I just mentioned to actually do something about it.

And then the last point I'd make is that in speech, there's an interesting distinction between the model being unfair because of the training distribution versus being unfair in a way that's really about the richness of the signal. Some accents or speaking styles are just underrepresented in the data, and that's a data collection problem you can fix by collecting more. But you can imagine cases where the acoustics themselves are genuinely harder, and then you have to be honest about the tradeoffs: you may be able to equalize error rates across groups, but only by accepting some degradation elsewhere. That's not a reason not to do it, but I think it's important to be clear-eyed that fairness in these settings is rarely free, and that the absence of labels doesn't make the underlying tradeoff go away. It just makes it harder to see.

r002.rationale: It flags concerns about inferring demographic attributes, but does not clearly advise against imputing traditional demographic categories for fairness assessment; it also suggests using a labeled audit set.

r003.rationale: It recommends finding and protecting groups defined by speech variation, including regional accents and speech impediments, and specifically mentions auditing accent or dialect.

astra-6.text:
Well, I think the first thing to recognize is that the absence of demographic labels doesn’t make the fairness problem go away. It makes it harder to measure. You can have very good average recognition accuracy and still have groups of speakers for whom the system works quite poorly.

One approach is to look for collections of speakers or acoustic conditions where the error rate is high, even if you don’t know the demographics of those collections. Can you improve performance for those groups instead of simply optimizing the average? That’s a useful direction, but it has a limitation: the groups you discover that way may not correspond to the demographic groups whose treatment you’re concerned about. So I wouldn’t equate that with demonstrating demographic fairness.

Ultimately, if you want to make a claim about fairness across particular demographic groups, you need some way to evaluate performance across those groups. That might mean collecting demographic information, with appropriate consent and privacy protections, for a separate evaluation set. You don’t necessarily need those attributes at prediction time, but without them even at evaluation time, you have to be quite careful about what you claim.

r002.rationale: It does not advise against imputing demographic categories; it instead suggests collecting demographic information for evaluation.

r003.rationale: It suggests examining high-error speaker groups or acoustic conditions, but does not recommend assessing fairness across naturally occurring speech variations such as accents or dialects.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, I think the first thing to recognize is that if you don’t have demographic annotations, you can’t simply conclude that your system is fair. You may not even be able to measure the particular disparities you care about. But that doesn’t mean there’s nothing you can do.

One approach is to look for groups of speakers on which the system performs poorly, without requiring those groups to correspond to a predefined demographic category. You might find, for example, that a particular set of speech patterns is associated with much higher recognition error. Then you can ask whether improving average accuracy is leaving those speakers behind, and adjust the learning objective to give their errors more weight.

The caveat is that this gives you a kind of robustness across groups, rather than a guarantee of demographic fairness. A grouping based on acoustic similarity may miss a socially important population. So I would view that as a useful approach when labels are unavailable, while still asking whether you can collect appropriate, consented demographic information for auditing. The distinction between improving performance for underserved speakers and actually verifying a fairness claim is important.

r002.rationale: It describes evaluating groups without predefined demographic labels, but does not clearly advise against imputing traditional demographic categories onto the data.
